title: HCF, LCM, squares, cubes and roots
summary: Use prime factorisation to find HCF, LCM, squares, cubes, square roots and cube roots.
objectives: Find the HCF and LCM of positive integers using prime factors.
Recognise and calculate square, cube, square-root and cube-root relationships.

sections.title: Use prime powers to compare factors and multiples

blocks.text: Prime factorisation exposes the building blocks of a positive integer. To find the highest common factor (HCF), take each prime shared by all the numbers with its smallest index. To find the lowest common multiple (LCM), take every prime that appears with its largest index. This works because an HCF must divide every number, while an LCM must contain enough of every prime factor to be divisible by every number.
For these two numbers, the common prime powers with the smaller indices give the HCF; all prime powers with the larger indices give the LCM.

sections.title: Squares, cubes and their inverse operations

blocks.text: Squaring multiplies a number by itself, while cubing multiplies three equal factors. A square root reverses squaring and a cube root reverses cubing. For positive numbers, the symbol
means the non-negative square root. A negative number has no real square root, but it can have a real cube root because three negative factors give a negative product.

sections.title: Choose the operation that matches the question

blocks.text: Use HCF when a quantity must be split into the largest equal groups or pieces with nothing left over. Use LCM when repeating events must meet again, or when finding the smallest quantity divisible by several given numbers. A quick check prevents the common reversal: an HCF cannot exceed the smallest input, whereas an LCM cannot be smaller than the largest positive input. For roots, estimate between nearby perfect squares or cubes before using a calculator.
